---
title: OAuth Connect
description: "Let your app act as a person in Pi Durable Platform: discovery, identifying your app with a metadata document or registration, scopes, authorization with PKCE, silent reconnects with prompt=none, the expected account with login_hint, tokens and subjects, refresh rotation and its grace, revocation, and handling 401s."
---

With **OAuth Connect**, a person connects your app to Pi Durable Platform once, and your app then calls the API **as that person**: their personal workspace, their teams' agents, their private threads. The platform is a small OAuth 2.1 authorization server and issues its own opaque tokens, so this works whatever identity provider the platform uses. Your app never sees the person's password or identity provider tokens.

All clients are **public**: no client secret on the authorization code flow. PKCE is required. (A trusted app can get an app secret from a platform admin, but only for its app-level endpoints: see [Apps with many people](/docs/build/apps-with-many-people).)

## 1. Discover

```sh
curl https://agents.example.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
```

returns the authorization server metadata (RFC 8414): the `issuer` (the platform's `APP_URL`), `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint`, `registration_endpoint`, `revocation_endpoint`, `scopes_supported: ["agents", "agents:read"]`, `code_challenge_methods_supported: ["S256"]`, `prompt_values_supported: ["none", "consent"]`, and `client_id_metadata_document_supported: true`.

`GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` (RFC 9728) names the resource (the same `APP_URL`) and its authorization server. `GET /v1/auth/config` also has a `connect` object with the endpoints; its presence is how an app can tell that a platform supports OAuth Connect.

## 2. Identify your app

Choose one.

### A Client ID Metadata Document (preferred)

Publish a JSON document at an `https` URL with a path, on your app's site, and use that URL as your `client_id`:

```json
{
  "client_id": "https://chat.example.com/oauth/client-metadata.json",
  "client_name": "Example Corp Chat",
  "redirect_uris": ["https://chat.example.com/connect/callback"],
  "client_uri": "https://chat.example.com",
  "logo_uri": "https://chat.example.com/logo.png"
}
```

- `client_id` must equal the document's URL exactly (at most 500 characters, no query or fragment).
- `redirect_uris` are `https`, or `http` on a loopback host.
- `client_uri` and `logo_uri` are optional and shown only when `https`. The platform serves the logo itself; see [The logo](#the-logo).

The platform's server fetches the document when someone starts a connection (not on token requests): from public addresses only, without redirects or proxies, within 5 seconds, at most 16 KiB, and it must answer `200` with `Content-Type: application/json`. Serve it exactly at that URL, with no sign-in or trailing-slash redirect in front. It is cached for its `Cache-Control: max-age`, between 1 minute and 1 hour (10 minutes without one; `no-store` or `no-cache` mean 1 minute), so a change applies when the cached copy expires.

Its host vouches for the name, and platform admins can mark such an app **trusted** so people skip the approval page. Don't list loopback redirect URIs in a production document: a trusted app's ID with a local redirect would let any local program get a code without the person seeing a page.

### The logo

The platform shows `logo_uri` (from a document or a registration) on the approval screen, in **Connected apps** and on a person's page in **Admin › Users**, but it **proxies** it (since v0.1.2): the console's Content-Security-Policy allows images only from the platform, so the browser never loads your address. The platform fetches the logo itself, checks it and serves it from its own origin at `GET /v1/oauth/client-logo?client_id=…`, to signed-in people only. The address is always the one in your document or registration, never one from the request.

- A public `https` address, with no redirects, and at most 256 KiB.
- PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, verified by their bytes. **No SVG.** A file that isn't what its bytes say is refused.
- Cached for an hour, so a new logo can take that long to appear.
- If the logo can't be loaded or isn't acceptable, the pages show your app's initials.
- With [several platform replicas](/docs/operate/replicas), each caches your document and logo on its own. The approval page loads the logo in a second request, which may reach a replica that hasn't fetched your document yet, so on some requests the page shows your app's initials instead.

### Dynamic Client Registration

For development, or apps without a site, register once (RFC 7591):

```sh
curl -X POST https://agents.example.com/oauth/register -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"client_name": "My dev app", "redirect_uris": ["http://localhost:5177/connect/callback"]}'
```

It returns a `client_id` starting `pdpcl_`. Keep it. A registered client unused for 30 days is deleted (an approval or a token, refreshes included, counts as use); register again then. Registered clients are never trusted, and the approval page says their name is unverified. Registration allows 10 requests a minute per address.

## 3. Send the person to authorize

Create a PKCE verifier and its S256 challenge, and a `state`, then send the person's browser to:

```text
https://agents.example.com/oauth/authorize
  ?response_type=code
  &client_id=https%3A%2F%2Fchat.example.com%2Foauth%2Fclient-metadata.json
  &redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fchat.example.com%2Fconnect%2Fcallback
  &state=…
  &code_challenge=…
  &code_challenge_method=S256
  &scope=agents
```

- `scope` is optional: `agents` (the default) or `agents:read`. See [Scopes](#scopes).
- `resource`, if you send it, must be the platform's `APP_URL` (otherwise `invalid_target`).
- `prompt` and `login_hint` are optional. See [Silent reconnects](#silent-reconnects-with-promptnone) and [The expected account](#the-expected-account-with-login_hint).
- Redirect URIs must match a registered one exactly, except that a **loopback** redirect matches on any port (RFC 8252). `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` are different hosts.
- A parameter given twice is an error. Others the platform doesn't use are ignored.

The person signs in to the platform as usual (so its sign-in rules, groups and suspension apply), then sees the approval page once. Approval is remembered, and trusted apps skip the page. Already signed in and approved, they come straight back without seeing anything. Do this as a top-level navigation the person starts, never in a hidden frame.

Errors about the client or the redirect URI are shown to the person as a page, never redirected. Later errors come back to your redirect URI.

On success the browser comes back with `code`, `state` and `iss`. **Check `state`, and check that `iss` is the issuer you discovered.**

### Scopes

| Scope | The app may |
|---|---|
| `agents` | Act as the person on the routes below: use and create agents, send messages, rename and delete threads. It includes `agents:read` |
| `agents:read` | The same routes, **reads only**: list agents and threads, read conversations, follow event streams, read usage, models and limits. No messages, no new threads, no changes |

An `agents:read` token gets `403 insufficient_scope` for every method but `GET` and `HEAD`, with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", scope="agents"`. The consent page then says the app "wants to read your agents" and will "never send messages or change anything", and **Connected apps** marks the connection **Read only**.

Asking for `agents` on a connection the person allowed for `agents:read` shows the consent page again (with `prompt=none`, `consent_required`); allowing widens the connection. Asking for `agents:read` on an `agents` connection is silent and gets read-only tokens.

### Silent reconnects with prompt=none

With `prompt=none` the platform never shows a page. If it can answer at once (the person is signed in, is the one `login_hint` names, and allowed your app before for these scopes, or your app is trusted), the code comes back as usual. Otherwise the browser comes back to your redirect URI, with `state` and `iss`, and one of these errors:

| `error` | Why | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `login_required` | Not signed in to the platform. Or, for an app the person connected before or a trusted app, signed in as someone other than `login_hint` | Send the person through without `prompt` |
| `consent_required` | Your app isn't trusted, and the person never connected it or hasn't allowed it for these scopes | Send the person through without `prompt` |
| `interaction_required` | Signed in, but the account can't use the platform now (suspended, or no longer in an allowed group) | Send the person through without `prompt`; they see why |

For an app that isn't trusted and that the signed-in person never connected, the answer is always `consent_required`: the platform doesn't compare `login_hint`, so no app can find out which account a browser is signed in as.

Use it to reconnect quietly when your app has lost its tokens, and fall back to the normal flow when it fails. It still needs a top-level navigation: never a hidden frame.

`prompt=consent` shows the consent page even when the app was allowed before or is trusted. `login`, `select_account` and any value combined with `none` are `invalid_request`: the platform can't make the identity provider sign the person in again or choose an account.

### The expected account with login_hint

If your app knows who should connect, send their email address (or their identity provider subject) as `login_hint`, at most 320 characters on one line (otherwise `invalid_request`).

- **Not signed in**: the platform passes the hint to the identity provider when it sends the person to sign in.
- **Signed in as that person** (the email matches, ignoring case, or the subject does): nothing changes.
- **Signed in as someone else**: the platform never connects that account, even for a trusted or remembered app. With `prompt=none` you get `login_required` if the person connected your app before or it's trusted, and `consent_required` otherwise. Without it, the consent page says whom your app expected and offers **Sign in as …** (it signs out and starts your request again, so the person signs in with the hint) or **Cancel** (`access_denied`). Allowing is refused (`409 account_mismatch`).

Check the `subject` in the token response, or `GET /v1/me`, against the account you expected all the same.

## 4. Exchange the code

```sh
curl -X POST https://agents.example.com/oauth/token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code \
  -d client_id=https://chat.example.com/oauth/client-metadata.json \
  -d code=$CODE -d redirect_uri=https://chat.example.com/connect/callback \
  -d code_verifier=$VERIFIER
```

```json
{
  "access_token": "pdpat_…",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "refresh_token": "pdprt_…",
  "scope": "agents",
  "subject": "3f6c1d2e-…"
}
```

A code lives 60 seconds and works once. The access token lasts **1 hour**, the refresh token **30 days**. Keep tokens on your server, encrypted; never in the browser.

`scope` is what you asked for, at most what the person allowed. `subject` is the person's ID **for your app**: a random UUID, not their email or platform user ID, the same each time they connect your app (even after disconnecting) and different for every app. `GET /v1/me` with the token returns it too, as `connectedApp.subject` with `connectedApp.clientId` and `connectedApp.scopes`. The app-level endpoints name people by it.

## 5. Call the API

```sh
curl https://agents.example.com/v1/agents -H "Authorization: Bearer pdpat_…"
```

The token acts as the person **without their platform role**. It reaches the agent routes, template listings, their teams' models, usage, limits and MCP servers, and `GET /v1/me`, `GET /v1/teams` and `GET /v1/teams/{team}`. It can't reach administration, members, keys, service accounts or connected apps. To give the person an agent, use `PUT …/agents/by-key/{key}` in their personal workspace (the team with `kind: personal` in `GET /v1/teams`), or `POST /v1/teams/{team}/agents` with an `Idempotency-Key`. See [Agents for your app's users](/docs/build/agents-by-key) and [Creating agents safely](/docs/build/creating-agents).

Every request checks the token, its connection and the person again: a suspended person, or one who left a team, loses that access at once. Requests count against the person's rate limit, shared with their browser and API keys. What your app does is recorded in the audit log as the person, via your app.

## 6. Refresh

```sh
curl -X POST https://agents.example.com/oauth/token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d grant_type=refresh_token -d client_id=… -d refresh_token=pdprt_…
```

Each refresh returns a **new pair** and retires the refresh token you sent. Keep only the newest. A refresh may send a narrower `scope` (`agents:read` on an `agents` connection), never a wider one (`invalid_scope`).

- **Within 30 seconds** of a refresh token's first use, presenting it again returns another valid pair. Nothing is revoked, and the first pair stays valid. This covers two of your servers refreshing at once.
- **After 30 seconds**, presenting a retired refresh token is treated as theft: the whole connection is revoked, all its tokens stop working, the answer is `invalid_grant`, and the person must connect again.
- A refresh doesn't end older access tokens; they expire after their hour.

With several replicas, refresh under a lock and re-read the stored pair after taking it: if another replica already refreshed, use its pair. Refresh when a token is needed and close to expiry, not on a timer for everyone. The token endpoint allows 60 requests a minute per client address; over it, `429` with `error: "slow_down"` and `Retry-After`.

## 7. Handle a refused token

A refused token gets `401` with the usual error envelope (code `unauthorized`) and:

```text
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://agents.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource", error="invalid_token"
```

That means expired, revoked or disconnected. Refresh once; if the refresh answers `400 {"error": "invalid_grant"}`, show the person a **Reconnect** step that starts again at step 3.

## 8. Revoke

```sh
curl -X POST https://agents.example.com/oauth/revoke \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" -d token=pdprt_… -d client_id=…
```

Revoking a **refresh token** ends the whole connection; an access token, only itself. The answer is `200` whatever the token. Revoke when the person disconnects in your app or their account in your app is removed. They can also disconnect your app themselves in the platform (**Connected apps**), and platform admins can disconnect it for them.

## Endpoints and errors

The protocol endpoints answer OAuth errors (`{"error", "error_description"}`), not the `/v1` envelope. See [OAuth endpoints](/docs/api/oauth-endpoints) for each one.
